metadata.title: Asymmetric variations of multifunctions with application to functional inclusions

nodes.name: Functional inclusion $X(t)\subset F(t,X(t))$ with initial condition
nodes.statement: As an application, we establish the existence of set-valued solutions $X(t)$ of bounded variation to the functional inclusion of the form $X(t)\subset F(t,X(t))$ satisfying the initial condition $X(t_0)=X_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Find a bounded-variation set-valued solution $X$ of $X(t)\subset F(t,X(t))$ with $X(t_0)=X_0$.

nodes.name: Hermes' selector theorem for Lipschitz and BV multifunctions
nodes.statement: In contrast to this, it was shown in \cite{Hermes} that a Lipschitz continuous multifunction $F$ on $[a,b]$ with compact images from $\Rb^N$ admits a Lipschitz continuous selector, whose Lipschitz constant does not exceed that of the multifunction; furthermore, if $F$ is only continuous and of bounded (Jordan) variation, then it admits a \emph{continuous\/} selector.
nodes.statement_short: A Lipschitz multifunction on $[a,b]$ with compact images in $\Rb^N$ has a Lipschitz selector; a continuous BV one has a continuous selector.
assumptions: a Lipschitz continuous multifunction $F$ on $[a,b]$ with compact images from $\Rb^N$
conclusions: admits a Lipschitz continuous selector, whose Lipschitz constant does not exceed that of the multifunction
if $F$ is only continuous and of bounded (Jordan) variation, then it admits a \emph{continuous\/} selector

nodes.name: Selector of bounded variation for BV multifunctions (Chistyakov 1997)
nodes.statement: Changing the compactness arguments to generalized Helly's pointwise selection principle, it was proved in \cite{JDCS} that a multifunction $F$ on $[a,b]$ of bounded Jordan variation with compact images from a Banach space admits a selector, whose total Jordan variation does not exceed that of $F$ and passes through a given point in the graph of~$F$.
nodes.statement_short: A BV multifunction on $[a,b]$ with compact images in a Banach space has a selector of no larger Jordan variation through a prescribed graph point.
assumptions: a multifunction $F$ on $[a,b]$ of bounded Jordan variation with compact images from a Banach space
conclusions: admits a selector, whose total Jordan variation does not exceed that of $F$ and passes through a given point in the graph of~$F$

nodes.name: Pompeiu excess
nodes.statement: Given two nonempty sets $X,Y\subset M$, the \emph{Pompeiu excess\/} ({\it {\'e}cart}, in French) {\it of $X$ over $Y$} is defined by (\cite[pp.~281--282]{Pomp}, \cite[Chapter~II]{CV}) \begin{equation*} e(X,Y)\equiv e_d(X,Y):=\sup_{x\in X}d(x,Y)=\inf\{r>0:X\subset\Oc_r(Y)\}, \end{equation*} where $d(x,Y):=\inf_{y\in Y}d(x,y)$ is the distance\footnote{$d(x,\es):=+\infty.$} from $x\in M$ to $Y$, and the set $\Oc_r(Y):=\{x\in M:d(x,Y)<r\}$ is the open $r$-neighbourhood\footnote{$\Oc_r(\es)\!:=\!\es$ for $r>0$; $e(\es,Y):=0$ for any $Y\subset M$, and $e(X,\es):=+\infty$ if $\es\!\ne\! X\!\subset\! M$.} of~$Y$, $r>0$ (if $Y=\{y\}$, $\Oc_r(y)\equiv\Oc_r(Y)$ is simply the open ball of radius $r$ centered at $y\in M$). Note that $e(X,Y)\ne e(Y,X)$ in general.
nodes.statement_short: $e(X,Y)=\sup_{x\in X}d(x,Y)$, the asymmetric excess of $X$ over $Y$.

nodes.name: Well-known properties of the Pompeiu excess
nodes.statement: The well-known properties of $e(\cdot,\cdot)$ are as follows. Given $X,Y,Z\subset M$: \par\vspace{2pt} (a) $e(X,Y)\!=\!0$ iff\footnote{`iff' means as usual `if and only if'.} $X\!\subset\!\ov{Y}$, where $\ov{Y}\!=\!\bigcap_{r>0}\Oc_r(Y)$ is the closure of $Y$~in~$M$; \par\vspace{2pt} (b) $e(X,Y)\le e(X,Z)+e(Z,Y)$ (triangle inequality for~$e$); \par\vspace{2pt} (c) $e(X,Y)<+\infty$ provided $X$ and $Y$ are bounded (and, in particular bounded and closed, or compact).
nodes.origin_citation: classical properties of the Pompeiu excess
nodes.statement_short: Vanishing excess characterises closure-inclusion, $e$ satisfies a triangle inequality, and $e$ is finite on bounded sets.
assumptions: Given $X,Y,Z\subset M$
conclusions: (c) $e(X,Y)<+\infty$ provided $X$ and $Y$ are bounded (and, in particular bounded and closed, or compact)

nodes.name: Pompeiu-Hausdorff distance
nodes.statement: The \emph{Pompeiu-Hausdorff distance\/} between two sets $X,Y\subset M$ is defined by (e.g., \cite{Pomp}, \cite[Chapter~II]{CV})\footnote{Pompeiu \cite{Pomp} symmetrized the excess $e$ by $d_P(X,Y)\!:=\!e(X,Y)\!+\!e(Y,X)$ (cf. also~\cite{Ber-Pac}).} \begin{equation*} d_H(X,Y)\!:=\max\{e(X,Y),e(Y,X)\}\!=\! \inf\{r\!>\!0:\mbox{$X\!\subset\!\Oc_r(Y)$\,and\,$Y\!\subset\!\Oc_r(X)$}\}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: $d_H(X,Y)=\max\{e(X,Y),e(Y,X)\}$, the symmetrisation of the Pompeiu excess.

nodes.name: $d_H$ is a metric on bcl$(M)$ and on c$(M)$
nodes.statement: It follows from (a), (b), and (c) above that $d_H$ is a \emph{metric\/} (with finite values), called the \emph{Pompeiu-Hausdorff metric}, on the family $\mbox{bcl}(M)$ of all nonempty \emph{bounded closed\/} subsets of $M$ and, in particular on the family $\mbox{c}(M)$ of all nonempty \emph{compact\/} subsets of~$M$.
nodes.statement_short: The Pompeiu-Hausdorff distance is a finite-valued metric on bounded closed sets, in particular on compact sets.
assumptions: It follows from (a), (b), and (c) above
conclusions: $d_H$ is a \emph{metric\/} (with finite values), called the \emph{Pompeiu-Hausdorff metric}, on the family $\mbox{bcl}(M)$ of all nonempty \emph{bounded closed\/} subsets of $M$ and, in particular on the family $\mbox{c}(M)$ of all nonempty \emph{compact\/} subsets of~$M$

nodes.name: Multifunction (set-valued mapping)
nodes.statement: A \emph{multifunction\/} (or \emph{set-valued mapping\/}) from a nonempty set $T$ into $M$ is a rule $F$, which assigns to each $t\in T$ a unique subset $F(t)\subset M$; in symbols, $F:T\to\mathcal{P}(M)$, where $\mathcal{P}(M)$ is the power set of $M$ (=\,the family of all subsets of~$M$).
nodes.origin_citation: standard set-valued analysis; cf. Aubin & Frankowska 1990
differentia: assigns to each $t\in T$ a unique subset $F(t)\subset M$

nodes.name: Set-valued selector
nodes.statement: A multifunction $\Gamma:T\to\mathcal{P}(M)$ is said to be a \emph{set-valued selector\/} of $F:T\to\mathcal{P}(M)$ on $T$ provided $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$ for all $t\in T$. Clearly, $F$ is a set-valued selector of itself.
nodes.origin_citation: standard set-valued analysis; cf. Repovš & Semenov 1998

nodes.name: Selector (selection)
nodes.statement: If $\Gamma:T\to M$ is single-valued and $\Gamma(t)\in F(t)$ for all $t\in T$, then $\Gamma$ is called a \emph{selector\/} (or \emph{selection\/}) of~$F$ on~$T$.

nodes.name: Multifunction of bounded variation and the (total) Jordan variation $\nV(F,T)$
nodes.statement: Of main interest in this paper are multifunctions $F:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ with $T$ a nonempty subset of the reals $\Rb$. Such an $F$ is said to be \emph{of bounded variation\/} (with respect to~$d_H$) provided its (total) \emph{Jordan variation\/} \begin{equation*} \nV(F,T)\!:=\sup_\pi\sum_{i=1}^m d_H\bigl(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i)\bigr)\quad \mbox{is finite\quad ($\nV(F,\es):=0$),} \end{equation*} the supremum being taken over all partitions $\pi$ of the set $T\subset\Rb$, i.e., $m\in\Nb$ and $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m\subset T$ such that $t_{i-1}\le t_i$ for all $i\in\{1,\dots,m\}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Jordan variation; cf. Chistyakov, Sbornik Math. 189 (1998)
nodes.statement_short: $F$ is of bounded variation when the sup over partitions of $\sum d_H(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))$ is finite.
nodes.genus: multifunctions $F:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ with $T$ a nonempty subset of the reals $\Rb$

nodes.name: Directional (excess) variations $\riV(F,T)$ and $\leV(F,T)$
nodes.statement: In order to do it, given $F:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$, following \cite{JMAA07} the quantities \begin{equation*} \riV(F,T)\!:=\!\sup_\pi\sum_{i=1}^m e\bigl(F(t_{i-1}\!),F(t_i)\bigr) \mbox{ and \,} \leV(F,T)\!:=\!\sup_\pi\sum_{i=1}^m e\bigl(F(t_i),F(t_{i-1}\!)\bigr) \end{equation*} are said to be the \emph{directional\/} (or \emph{excess\/}) \emph{variations of $F$ to the right\/} and \emph{to the left}, respectively ($\riV(F,\es)=\leV(F,\es):=0$).
nodes.statement_short: One-sided variations built from the asymmetric excess $e$ instead of the symmetric $d_H$.
nodes.definiendum: directional (or excess) variations of $F$ to the right and to the left

nodes.name: Comparison of directional variations with the Jordan variation
nodes.statement: Clearly, \begin{equation*} \max\bigl\{\riV(F,T),\leV(F,T)\bigr\}\le\nV(F,T)\le\riV(F,T)+\leV(F,T), \end{equation*} and so, $\nV(F,T)$ is finite iff both $\riV(F,T)$ and $\leV(F,T)$ are finite.
nodes.statement_short: $\max\{\riV,\leV\}\le\nV\le\riV+\leV$, so $\nV$ is finite iff both directional variations are.
conclusions: $\nV(F,T)$ is finite iff both $\riV(F,T)$ and $\leV(F,T)$ are finite

nodes.name: Road interpretation of the main theorem
nodes.statement: A somewhat free and intuitive interpretation of Theorem~\ref{t:BV} can be given as follows. We may imagine $F$ to be a road with the value $F(t)$ as a section at a given coordinate~$t$. If $t$ increases, the section $F(t)$ moves in one direction, say, to the right. Theorem~\ref{t:BV} asserts that if the road $F$ is properly built/controlled (i.e., its variation to the right is finite), then an extended object (e.g., a car) can freely pass it.
nodes.statement_short: If a road $F$ is well built to the right, an extended object can pass it.

nodes.name: Monotonicity characterisation of vanishing variations
nodes.statement: By the definition of $\nV$, $\nV(F,T)=0$ iff $F$ is constant on $T$. The definition of~$\riV$ and property (a) of $e$ in Section~\ref{s:mr} imply $\riV(F,T)=0$ iff $F$ is \emph{nondecreasing\/} on $T$ in the sense that $F(s)\subset F(t)$ for all $s,t\in T$ with $s\le t$. Similarly, $\leV(F,T)=0$ iff $F$ is \emph{nonincresing\/} on $T$, i.e., $F(s)\supset F(t)$ for all $s,t\in T$,~$s\le t$.
nodes.statement_short: $\nV=0$ iff $F$ constant, $\riV=0$ iff $F$ nondecreasing, $\leV=0$ iff $F$ nonincreasing.
assumptions: Let $T\subset\Rb$ and $F:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ be a multifunction.
conclusions: $\riV(F,T)=0$ iff $F$ is \emph{nondecreasing\/} on $T$ in the sense that $F(s)\subset F(t)$ for all $s,t\in T$ with $s\le t$
$\leV(F,T)=0$ iff $F$ is \emph{nonincresing\/} on $T$, i.e., $F(s)\supset F(t)$ for all $s,t\in T$,~$s\le t$

nodes.name: Additivity of the Jordan variation $\nV$
nodes.origin_citation: Chistyakov, The Variation (1992) 2.19; J. Dynam. Control Systems 1997; Sbornik Math. 1998
nodes.statement_short: $\nV$ splits additively at every point of $T$.
assumptions: Since $(\mbox{c}(M),d_H)$ is a metric space

nodes.name: Additivity also holds for the directional variations $\riV$ and $\leV$
nodes.statement: We assert that the additivity property \eq{e:Vadd} holds also for $\riV$ and $\leV$ in place of~$\nV$. Since the Hausdorff excess $e$ is not symmetric, we have to take care of the order of its arguments. So, we explicitly verify \eq{e:Vadd} at least for~$\riV$.
nodes.statement_short: The additivity identity carries over to the one-sided excess variations, with care for the order of the arguments of $e$.
conclusions: the additivity property \eq{e:Vadd} holds also for $\riV$ and $\leV$ in place of~$\nV$

nodes.name: Proof (of additivity of $\riV$)
nodes.statement: Given $\xi,\eta\in\Rb$ such that $\xi<\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$ and $\eta<\riV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})$, there are $m,n\in\Nb$, a partition $\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$ with $t_m=t$ and a partition $\{s_j\}_{j=0}^n$ of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$ with $s_0=t$ such that \begin{equation} \xi<\sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))\quad\mbox{and}\quad \eta<\sum_{j=1}^n e(F(s_{j-1}),F(s_j)). \end{equation} Since $\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m\cup\{s_j\}_{j=0}^n$ is a partition of $T$, we get, from \eq{e:xi1}, $\xi+\eta<\riV(F,T)$, which, due to the arbitrariness of $\xi$ and $\eta$ as above, implies the inequality \begin{equation*} \riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+\riV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})\le\riV(F,T). \end{equation*} In order to prove the reverse inequality, let $\xi\in\Rb$ be arbitrary such that $\xi<\riV(F,T)$. Then, there are $m\in\Nb$ and a partition $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T$ such that the first inequality in \eq{e:xi1} holds. If $t_m\le t$, then $\pi$ is a partition of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$, and if $t\le t_0$, then $\pi$ is a partition of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$, and so, in the either case, the first inequality in \eq{e:xi1} implies \begin{equation} \xi<\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+\riV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)}). \end{equation} Now, suppose $t_{k-1}\le t\le t_k$ for some $k\in\{1,\dots,m\}$. By the triangle inequality for~$e$, we have \begin{equation} e(F(t_{k-1}),F(t_k))\le e(F(t_{k-1}),F(t))+e(F(t),F(t_k)). \end{equation} Since $\{t_i\}_{i=0}^{k-1}\cup\{t\}$ is a partition of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$ and $\{t\}\cup\{t_i\}_{i=k}^m$ is a partition of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$, from the first inequality in \eq{e:xi1} and \eq{e:kk}, once again we get \eq{e:x2}. By the arbitrariness of $\xi<\riV(F,T)$, \eq{e:x2} implies \begin{equation*} \riV(F,T)\le\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+\riV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)}), \end{equation*} which was to be proved.
nodes.statement_short: Two-sided estimate: refine partitions on each side for $\ge$, then split an arbitrary partition at $t$ using the triangle inequality for $e$ for $\le$.

nodes.name: Lower bound by juxtaposing one-sided partitions
nodes.statement: Given $\xi,\eta\in\Rb$ such that $\xi<\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$ and $\eta<\riV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})$, there are $m,n\in\Nb$, a partition $\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$ with $t_m=t$ and a partition $\{s_j\}_{j=0}^n$ of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$ with $s_0=t$ such that \begin{equation} \xi<\sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))\quad\mbox{and}\quad \eta<\sum_{j=1}^n e(F(s_{j-1}),F(s_j)). \end{equation} Since $\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m\cup\{s_j\}_{j=0}^n$ is a partition of $T$, we get, from \eq{e:xi1}, $\xi+\eta<\riV(F,T)$, which, due to the arbitrariness of $\xi$ and $\eta$ as above, implies the inequality \begin{equation*} \riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+\riV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})\le\riV(F,T). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Concatenate near-optimal partitions of the two halves to get $\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+\riV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})\le\riV(F,T)$.

nodes.name: Reverse inequality: partition lying entirely on one side
nodes.statement: In order to prove the reverse inequality, let $\xi\in\Rb$ be arbitrary such that $\xi<\riV(F,T)$. Then, there are $m\in\Nb$ and a partition $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T$ such that the first inequality in \eq{e:xi1} holds. If $t_m\le t$, then $\pi$ is a partition of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$, and if $t\le t_0$, then $\pi$ is a partition of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$, and so, in the either case, the first inequality in \eq{e:xi1} implies \begin{equation} \xi<\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+\riV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: If the partition does not straddle $t$ it is already a partition of one half, giving the bound directly.

nodes.name: Reverse inequality: straddling partition split at $t$
nodes.statement: Now, suppose $t_{k-1}\le t\le t_k$ for some $k\in\{1,\dots,m\}$. By the triangle inequality for~$e$, we have \begin{equation} e(F(t_{k-1}),F(t_k))\le e(F(t_{k-1}),F(t))+e(F(t),F(t_k)). \end{equation} Since $\{t_i\}_{i=0}^{k-1}\cup\{t\}$ is a partition of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$ and $\{t\}\cup\{t_i\}_{i=k}^m$ is a partition of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$, from the first inequality in \eq{e:xi1} and \eq{e:kk}, once again we get \eq{e:x2}. By the arbitrariness of $\xi<\riV(F,T)$, \eq{e:x2} implies \begin{equation*} \riV(F,T)\le\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+\riV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)}), \end{equation*} which was to be proved.
nodes.statement_short: Insert $t$ into the straddling interval and apply the triangle inequality for $e$ to conclude.

nodes.name: Variation functions $v_F$, $\ori{v}_F$, $\ole{v}_F$
nodes.statement: Recall that the function $v_F(t)\!:=\!\nV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$, $t\!\in\! T$, is said to be the {\it var\-i\-a\-tion function\/} of $F$ on~$T$. We define the \emph{variation function\/} of $F$ to the right (to the left) by $\ori{v}_F(t):=\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$ (by $\ole{v}_F(t):=\leV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$, respectively) for all $t\in T$. Clearly, $v_F,\ori{v}_F,\ole{v}_F:T\to[0,+\infty]$ are \emph{nondecreasing\/} on~$T$. If $F$ is clear from the context, we omit the subscript $F$ and write $v$, $\ori{v}$, and $\ole{v}$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Nondecreasing functions recording the variation (total, right, left) accumulated up to $t$.
nodes.definiendum: variation function of $F$ to the right (to the left)

nodes.name: Lemma 1 (characterisation of bounded directional variation)
nodes.statement: Given $F:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$, $\riV(F,T)<+\infty$ iff there is a nondecreasing bounded function $\varphi:T\to\Rb$ such that $e(F(s),F(t))\le\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)$ for all $s,t\in T$ with $s\le t;$ moreover, $\riV(F,T)\le\nV(\varphi,T)$. {\rm(}A similar assertion holds for $\leV(F,T)<+\infty$ if the inequality is written as $e(F(t),F(s))\le\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)$.{\rm)}
nodes.statement_short: $\riV(F,T)<\infty$ iff a nondecreasing bounded $\varphi$ dominates the excess increments, and then $\riV(F,T)\le\nV(\varphi,T)$.
assumptions: Given $F:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$
conclusions: $\riV(F,T)<+\infty$ iff there is a nondecreasing bounded function $\varphi:T\to\Rb$ such that $e(F(s),F(t))\le\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)$ for all $s,t\in T$ with $s\le t;$
{\rm(}A similar assertion holds for $\leV(F,T)<+\infty$ if the inequality is written as $e(F(t),F(s))\le\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)$.{\rm)}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: ($\Rightarrow\!$) Let $\ori{v}(t)=\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$, $t\in T$, be the variation function (to the right) of~$F$. It is nondecreasing on $T$ and bounded: $\sup_{t\in T}\ori{v}(t)\le\riV(F,T)$. Given $s,t\in T$, $s\le t$, the additivity of $\riV$ implies \begin{equation*} e(F(s),F(t))\le\riV(F,T_{[s,t]})=\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})-\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,s]}) =\ori{v}(t)-\ori{v}(s). \end{equation*} It remains to set $\varphi:=\ori{v}$. ($\!\Leftarrow$) Let $m\in\Nb$ and $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ be a partition of $T$. Since $t_{i-1}\le t_i$ for all $i=1,\dots,m$, by the assumption we get \begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^me(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))&\le\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(\varphi(t_i)-\varphi(t_{i-1})\bigr) =\varphi(t_m)-\varphi(t_0)\\ &\le\sup_{t\in T}\varphi(t)-\inf_{s\in T}\varphi(s)=\nV(\varphi,T)<+\infty. \end{align*} It remains to take the supremum over all partitions $\pi$ of $T$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $\varphi=\ori{v}$ for the forward direction; telescope the dominating increments over an arbitrary partition for the converse.

nodes.name: Forward direction: take $\varphi:=\ori{v}$
nodes.statement: ($\Rightarrow\!$) Let $\ori{v}(t)=\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$, $t\in T$, be the variation function (to the right) of~$F$. It is nondecreasing on $T$ and bounded: $\sup_{t\in T}\ori{v}(t)\le\riV(F,T)$. Given $s,t\in T$, $s\le t$, the additivity of $\riV$ implies \begin{equation*} e(F(s),F(t))\le\riV(F,T_{[s,t]})=\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})-\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,s]}) =\ori{v}(t)-\ori{v}(s). \end{equation*} It remains to set $\varphi:=\ori{v}$.
nodes.statement_short: The right variation function is nondecreasing, bounded, and dominates $e(F(s),F(t))$ by additivity.

nodes.name: Converse direction: telescoping over a partition
nodes.statement: ($\!\Leftarrow$) Let $m\in\Nb$ and $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ be a partition of $T$. Since $t_{i-1}\le t_i$ for all $i=1,\dots,m$, by the assumption we get \begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^me(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))&\le\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(\varphi(t_i)-\varphi(t_{i-1})\bigr) =\varphi(t_m)-\varphi(t_0)\\ &\le\sup_{t\in T}\varphi(t)-\inf_{s\in T}\varphi(s)=\nV(\varphi,T)<+\infty. \end{align*} It remains to take the supremum over all partitions $\pi$ of $T$.
nodes.statement_short: Sum the dominating increments telescopically and take the supremum over partitions.

nodes.name: Total boundedness of the image fails under directional variation alone
nodes.statement: It is known (\cite[1.23]{Var}, \cite[Lemma~11]{MZ}) that if $F:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ and $\nV(F,T)\!<\!+\infty$, then the image $F(T):=\bigcup_{t\in T}F(t)$ is a \emph{totally bounded\/} (hence separable) subset of~$M$ (if, in addition, $(M,d)$ is complete, then the closure of $F(T)$ in $M$ is compact). However, condition $\nV(F,T)\!<\!+\infty$ cannot be replaced neither by $\riV(F,T)\!<\!+\infty$ nor by $\leV(F,T)\!<\!+\infty$ (see Example~\ref{ex:5.5}).
nodes.statement_short: $\nV(F,T)<\infty$ forces $F(T)$ totally bounded, but neither $\riV<\infty$ nor $\leV<\infty$ suffices.

nodes.name: Sequential lower semicontinuity of $\nV$
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise $d_H$-convergence implies $\nV(F,T)\le\liminf_n\nV(F_n,T)$.
assumptions: If a sequence $\{F_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ of multifunctions $F_n:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ \emph{converges in $\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ pointwise on $T$} to $F$

nodes.name: Lower semicontinuity also holds for $\riV$ and $\leV$
nodes.statement: We assert that \eq{e:Vsem} is valid for $\riV$ and $\leV$ in place of $\nV$, as well.
nodes.statement_short: The liminf inequality carries over to the directional variations.
conclusions: \eq{e:Vsem} is valid for $\riV$ and $\leV$ in place of $\nV$, as well

nodes.name: Proof (of lower semicontinuity of $\riV$)
nodes.statement: For any $n\in\Nb$ and $s,t\in T$, the triangle inequality for $e$ implies \begin{equation*} |e(F_n(s),F_n(t))-e(F(s),F(t))|\le d_H(F_n(s),F(s))+d_H(F_n(t),F(t)), \end{equation*} and so, by the pointwise convergence of $F_n$ to $F$, $e(F_n(s),F_n(t))\!\to\! e(F(s),F(t))$ as $n\to\infty$. Given $m\in\Nb$ and a partition $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T$, by definition of~$\riV$, \begin{equation*} \sum_{i=1}^m e(F_n(t_{i-1}),F_n(t_i))\le\riV(F_n,T)\quad\mbox{for all \,\,$n\in\Nb$.} \end{equation*} Passing to the limit inferior as $n\to\infty$, we get \begin{equation*} \sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\riV(F_n,T), \end{equation*} and it remains to take the supremum over all partitions $\pi$ of $T$.
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise convergence makes each excess term converge; bound partition sums by $\riV(F_n,T)$, pass to the liminf, then take the supremum over partitions.

nodes.name: Convergence of the excess along the sequence
nodes.statement: For any $n\in\Nb$ and $s,t\in T$, the triangle inequality for $e$ implies \begin{equation*} |e(F_n(s),F_n(t))-e(F(s),F(t))|\le d_H(F_n(s),F(s))+d_H(F_n(t),F(t)), \end{equation*} and so, by the pointwise convergence of $F_n$ to $F$, $e(F_n(s),F_n(t))\!\to\! e(F(s),F(t))$ as $n\to\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: The triangle inequality for $e$ gives $e(F_n(s),F_n(t))\to e(F(s),F(t))$.

nodes.name: Uniform partition bound by $\riV(F_n,T)$
nodes.statement: Given $m\in\Nb$ and a partition $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T$, by definition of~$\riV$, \begin{equation*} \sum_{i=1}^m e(F_n(t_{i-1}),F_n(t_i))\le\riV(F_n,T)\quad\mbox{for all \,\,$n\in\Nb$.} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Every partition sum for $F_n$ is bounded by $\riV(F_n,T)$.

nodes.name: Pass to the limit inferior and take the supremum
nodes.statement: Passing to the limit inferior as $n\to\infty$, we get \begin{equation*} \sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\riV(F_n,T), \end{equation*} and it remains to take the supremum over all partitions $\pi$ of $T$.
nodes.statement_short: Take liminf in $n$ and then the supremum over partitions of $T$.

nodes.name: Limit equalities for the variation at an unattained endpoint
nodes.origin_citation: Chistyakov, The Variation (1992); J. Dynam. Control Systems 1997
nodes.statement_short: $\nV(F,T)$ is the limit of the variations over truncations when $\sup T$ (resp. $\inf T$) is not attained.
assumptions: if $s\!=\!\sup T\!\in\!\Rb\cup\{+\infty\}$ and $s\!\notin\! T$
if \,$i\!=\!\inf T\!\in\Rb\cup\{-\infty\}$ \,and $i\!\notin\! T$

nodes.name: The limit equalities hold for $\riV$ and $\leV$ as well
nodes.statement: We are going to show that these assertions hold for $\riV$ and $\leV$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: The endpoint limit identities transfer to the directional variations.
conclusions: these assertions hold for $\riV$ and $\leV$ as well

nodes.name: Existence of the limit by monotonicity
nodes.statement: Since $\ori{v}$ is nondecreasing on $T$, the limit on the right in \eq{e:ttos} (with $\nV$ replaced by~$\riV$) exists in $[0,+\infty]$ and is equal to $\sup_{t\in T}\ori{v}(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: The limit exists in $[0,+\infty]$ and equals $\sup_{t\in T}\ori{v}(t)$ since $\ori{v}$ is nondecreasing.

nodes.name: Easy inequality $\lim\ori{v}\le\riV(F,T)$
nodes.statement: Given $t\in T$, we have $T_{(-\infty,t]}\subset T$, and so, $\ori{v}(t)\le\riV(F,T)$, which implies $\lim_{T\ni t\to s}\ori{v}(t)\le\riV(F,T)$.
nodes.statement_short: Each truncation is contained in $T$, so $\ori{v}(t)\le\riV(F,T)$.

nodes.name: Converse inequality via an approximating partition
nodes.statement: Conversely, given $\xi\in\Rb$ with $\xi<\riV(F,T)$, there are $m\in\Nb$ and a partition $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T$ (and so, \mbox{$t_0\le t_1\le\dots\le t_{m-1}\le t_m<s$}) such that \begin{equation*} \xi<\sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))\le\ori{v}(t_m)\le\lim_{T\ni t\to s}\ori{v}(t). \end{equation*} Passing to the limit as $\xi\to\riV(F,T)$, we get $\riV(F,T)\le\lim_{T\ni t\to s}\ori{v}(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Any $\xi<\riV(F,T)$ is dominated by a partition sum below $\lim\ori{v}(t)$.

nodes.name: Left/right limit point and left/right isolated point of $T$
nodes.statement: We say that $t\in\Rb$ is a \emph{left\/} (\emph{right\/}) \emph{limit point\/} of~$T$ if $T_{(t-\vep,t)}\ne\es$ (respectively, $T_{(t,t+\vep)}\ne\es$) for all $\vep>0$. A point $t\in T$, which is not a left (or right) limit point of $T$, is called the \emph{left\/} (or \emph{right\/}) \emph{isolated point\/} of~$T$.

nodes.name: Jump formulas for the variation function $v$
nodes.statement:
By virtue of \cite[Lemma~4.2]{MatSb}, the following two assertions hold.  egin{itemize} \item[{m(a)}] If $t\in T$ is a left limit point of $T$ and $
V(F,T)<+\infty$, then  egin{equation} v(t)=v(t-0)+\lim_{T
i s	o t-0}d_H(F(s),F(t)). ootnote{$v(t-0):=\lim_{T
i s	o t-0}v(s)$ is the left limit of $v$ at $t$ along $T$, i.e., $v(t-0)$ is the limit of $v(s)$ as $s	o t$ with $s\in T_{(-\infty,t)}$.} \end{equation} \item[{m(b)}] If $t\in T$ is a right limit point of $T$ and $

If $t\in T$ is a right limit point of $T$ and $\nV(F,T)<+\infty$

nodes.name: Left (right) jump of $F$ at $t$
nodes.statement: The second limit in the right-hand side of \eq{e:VFtm} (of \eq{e:VF+0}) is known as the \emph{left\/} (\emph{right\/}, respectively) \emph{jump\/} of $F$ at~$t$.
nodes.genus: The second limit in the right-hand side of \eq{e:VFtm} (of \eq{e:VF+0})

If $t\in T$ is a left limit point of $T$, then ootnote{The limit superior in ($\ori{\mbox{m a}}$) is the limit of $\sup\{e(F(s),F(t)):s\in T_{(t-\vep,t)}\}$ as $\vep	o+0$; in ($\ole{\mbox{m a}}$) the limit superior is understood similarly.}  egin{itemize} \item[${m(\ori{\mbox{m a}})}$] $\ori{v}(t)=\ori{v}(t-0)+\displaystyle \limsup_{T

If $t\in T$ is a right limit point of $T$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement:
We concentrate on ($\ori{\mbox{m a}}$) and ($\ori{\mbox{m b}}$), making only remarks on ($\ole{\mbox{m a}}$) and ($\ole{\mbox{m b}}$). ($\ori{\mbox{m a}}$) First, we prove inequality $\ge$ in ($\ori{\mbox{m a}}$). By the additivity of $iV$, given $s\in T$ with $s<t$, we have  egin{equation*} \ori{v}(s)+e(F(s),F(t))\le\ori{v}(s)+iV(F,T_{[s,t]})=\ori{v}(t). \end{equation*} Since $\ori{v}$ is nondecreasing and bounded on $T$ (by $iV(F,T)$), and $t$ is a left limit point of $T$, the left limit $\ori{v}(t-0)$ exists in $[0,+\infty)$ and is equal to $\sup\{\ori{v}(s):s\in T,s<t\}$. Inequality $\ge$ in ($\ori{\mbox{m a}}$) follows now from the properties of the limit superior as $T\!
i\! s\!	o\! t\!-\!0$, since the right-hand side in ($\ori{\mbox{m a}}$) is equal to  egin{equation*} \lim_{T
i s	o t-0}\!\ori{v}(s)\!+\!\limsup_{T
i s	o t-0}\!e(F(s),F(t))\!=\! \limsup_{T
i s	o t-0}\! igl(\ori{v}(s)\!+\!e(F(s),F(t)) igr)\le\ori{v}(t). \end{equation*} Now we show that inequality $\le$ holds in ($\ori{\mbox{m a}}$). By the definition of $\ori{v}(t)$, which is finite, for any $\xi\in\Rb$, $\xi<\ori{v}(t)$, there are $m\in\Nb$ and a partition $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m\cup\{t\}$ of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$ with $t_m<t$ such that  egin{equation*} \xi<\sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))+e(F(t_m),F(t)). \end{equation*} Given $s\in T_{(t_m,t)}$, the triangle inequality for $e$ implies  egin{equation*} e(F(t_m),F(t))\le e(F(t_m),F(s))+e(F(s),F(t)), \end{equation*} and so, $\xi<\ori{v}(s)+e(F(s),F(t))$. Passing to the limit superior as $T
i s	o t-0$, we get  egin{equation*} \xi\le\ori{v}(t-0)+\limsup_{T
i s	o t-0}e(F(s),F(t)). \end{equation*} It remains to take into account the arbitrariness of $\xi<\ori{v}(t)$. \smallbreak ($\ori{\mbox{m b}}$) In order to prove inequality $\ge$ in ($\ori{\mbox{m b}}$), we make use of the additivity of $iV$ to get  egin{equation*} \ori{v}(t)+e(F(t),F(s))\le\ori{v}(t)+iV(F,T_{[t,s]})=\ori{v}(s)\quad \mbox{for all $s\in T_{(t,+\infty)}$.} \end{equation*} Now, it suffices to pass to the limit superior as $T
i s	o t+0$. To show inequality $\le$ in ($\ori{\mbox{m b}}$), we apply the additivity property of $iV$ several times. To begin with, note that  egin{equation} iV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})=iV(F,T)-\ori{v}(t). \end{equation} Given $\xi\in\Rb$ with $\xi<iV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})$, there exist $m\in\Nb$ and a partition $\{t\}\cup\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$ with $t<t_0$ such that  egin{equation*} \xi<e(F(t),F(t_0))+\sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i)). \end{equation*} Since, for any $s\!\in\! T_{(t,t_0)}$, $e(F(t),F(t_0))\!\le\! e(F(t),F(s))\!+\!e(F(s),F(t_0))$, we~find  egin{align*} \xi+\ori{v}(t_m)-iV(F,T)\le\xi&<e(F(t),F(s))+iV(F,T_{[s,t_m]})\[2pt] &=e(F(t),F(s))+\ori{v}(t_m)-\ori{v}(s), \end{align*} and so, $\ori{v}(s)\le(iV(F,T)-\xi)+e(F(t),F(s))$. Passing to the limit superior as $T
i s	o t+0$, we get  egin{equation*} \ori{v}(t+0)\leiV(F,T)-\xi+\limsup_{T
i s	o t+0}e(F(t),F(s)). \end{equation*} It remains to let $\xi$ tend to the value \eq{e:tin}. \smallbreak ($\ole{\mbox{m a}}$), ($\ole{\mbox{m b}}$) Here we note only that, by the additivity of $\leV$,  egin{align*} \ole{v}(s)+e(F(t),F(s))\le\ole{v}(s)+\leV(F,T_{[s,t]})=\ole{v}(t)\quad  orall\,s\in T_{(-\infty,t)},\[2pt] \ole{v}(t)+e(F(s),F(t))\le\ole{v}(t)+\leV(F,T_{[t,s]})=\ole{v}(s)\quad  orall\,s\in T_{(t,+\infty)}, \end{align*} respectively.

nodes.name: Inequality $\ge$ in $(\ori{a})$
nodes.statement:
($\ori{\mbox{m a}}$) First, we prove inequality $\ge$ in ($\ori{\mbox{m a}}$). By the additivity of $iV$, given $s\in T$ with $s<t$, we have  egin{equation*} \ori{v}(s)+e(F(s),F(t))\le\ori{v}(s)+iV(F,T_{[s,t]})=\ori{v}(t). \end{equation*} Since $\ori{v}$ is nondecreasing and bounded on $T$ (by $iV(F,T)$), and $t$ is a left limit point of $T$, the left limit $\ori{v}(t-0)$ exists in $[0,+\infty)$ and is equal to $\sup\{\ori{v}(s):s\in T,s<t\}$. Inequality $\ge$ in ($\ori{\mbox{m a}}$) follows now from the properties of the limit superior as $T\!
i\! s\!	o\! t\!-\!0$, since the right-hand side in ($\ori{\mbox{m a}}$) is equal to  egin{equation*} \lim_{T
i s	o t-0}\!\ori{v}(s)\!+\!\limsup_{T
i s	o t-0}\!e(F(s),F(t))\!=\! \limsup_{T
i s	o t-0}\! igl(\ori{v}(s)\!+\!e(F(s),F(t)) igr)\le\ori{v}(t). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Additivity gives $\ori{v}(s)+e(F(s),F(t))\le\ori{v}(t)$; pass to the limit superior.

nodes.name: Inequality $\le$ in $(\ori{a})$
nodes.statement: Now we show that inequality $\le$ holds in ($\ori{\mbox{\rm a}}$). By the definition of $\ori{v}(t)$, which is finite, for any $\xi\in\Rb$, $\xi<\ori{v}(t)$, there are $m\in\Nb$ and a partition $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m\cup\{t\}$ of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$ with $t_m<t$ such that \begin{equation*} \xi<\sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))+e(F(t_m),F(t)). \end{equation*} Given $s\in T_{(t_m,t)}$, the triangle inequality for $e$ implies \begin{equation*} e(F(t_m),F(t))\le e(F(t_m),F(s))+e(F(s),F(t)), \end{equation*} and so, $\xi<\ori{v}(s)+e(F(s),F(t))$. Passing to the limit superior as $T\ni s\to t-0$, we get \begin{equation*} \xi\le\ori{v}(t-0)+\limsup_{T\ni s\to t-0}e(F(s),F(t)). \end{equation*} It remains to take into account the arbitrariness of $\xi<\ori{v}(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $\ori{v}(t)$ by a partition, insert an intermediate $s$ via the triangle inequality for $e$, then take the limit superior.

nodes.name: Inequality $\ge$ in $(\ori{b})$
nodes.statement: ($\ori{\mbox{\rm b}}$) In order to prove inequality $\ge$ in ($\ori{\mbox{\rm b}}$), we make use of the additivity of $\riV$ to get \begin{equation*} \ori{v}(t)+e(F(t),F(s))\le\ori{v}(t)+\riV(F,T_{[t,s]})=\ori{v}(s)\quad \mbox{for all $s\in T_{(t,+\infty)}$.} \end{equation*} Now, it suffices to pass to the limit superior as $T\ni s\to t+0$.
nodes.statement_short: Additivity gives $\ori{v}(t)+e(F(t),F(s))\le\ori{v}(s)$ for $s>t$.

nodes.name: Inequality $\le$ in $(\ori{b})$
nodes.statement: To show inequality $\le$ in ($\ori{\mbox{\rm b}}$), we apply the additivity property of $\riV$ several times. To begin with, note that \begin{equation} \riV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})=\riV(F,T)-\ori{v}(t). \end{equation} Given $\xi\in\Rb$ with $\xi<\riV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})$, there exist $m\in\Nb$ and a partition $\{t\}\cup\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$ with $t<t_0$ such that \begin{equation*} \xi<e(F(t),F(t_0))+\sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i)). \end{equation*} Since, for any $s\!\in\! T_{(t,t_0)}$, $e(F(t),F(t_0))\!\le\! e(F(t),F(s))\!+\!e(F(s),F(t_0))$, we~find \begin{align*} \xi+\ori{v}(t_m)-\riV(F,T)\le\xi&<e(F(t),F(s))+\riV(F,T_{[s,t_m]})\\[2pt] &=e(F(t),F(s))+\ori{v}(t_m)-\ori{v}(s), \end{align*} and so, $\ori{v}(s)\le(\riV(F,T)-\xi)+e(F(t),F(s))$. Passing to the limit superior as $T\ni s\to t+0$, we get \begin{equation*} \ori{v}(t+0)\le\riV(F,T)-\xi+\limsup_{T\ni s\to t+0}e(F(t),F(s)). \end{equation*} It remains to let $\xi$ tend to the value \eq{e:tin}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply additivity repeatedly to $\riV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})=\riV(F,T)-\ori{v}(t)$ and let $\xi$ tend to that value.

nodes.name: The left-hand analogues $(\ole{a})$, $(\ole{b})$
nodes.statement: ($\ole{\mbox{\rm a}}$), ($\ole{\mbox{\rm b}}$) Here we note only that, by the additivity of $\leV$, \begin{align*} \ole{v}(s)+e(F(t),F(s))\le\ole{v}(s)+\leV(F,T_{[s,t]})=\ole{v}(t)\quad \forall\,s\in T_{(-\infty,t)},\\[2pt] \ole{v}(t)+e(F(s),F(t))\le\ole{v}(t)+\leV(F,T_{[t,s]})=\ole{v}(s)\quad \forall\,s\in T_{(t,+\infty)}, \end{align*} respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Same argument with the additivity chain for $\leV$ and the arguments of $e$ swapped.

nodes.name: Lemma 3 (open/closed endpoint jump formulas for $\riV$ and $\leV$)
nodes.statement:
If $t\in T$ is a left limit point of $T$, then  egin{itemize} \item[${m(\ori{\mbox{m a}})}$] $iV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})\!=\!iV(F,T_{(-\infty,t)})\!+\!\displaystyle \limsup_{T
i s	o t-0}e(F(s),F(t))$ \,if \,\,$iV(F,T)\!<\!+\infty;$ \item[${m(\ole{\mbox{m a}})}$] $\leV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})\!=\!\leV(F,T_{(-\infty,t)})\!+\!\displaystyle \limsup_{T
i s	o t-0}e(F(t),F(s))$ \,if \,\,$\leV(F,T)<+\infty.$ \end{itemize} If $t\in T$ is a right limit point of $T$, then  egin{itemize} \item[${m(\ori{\mbox{m b}})}$] $iV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})\!=\!iV(F,T_{(t,+\infty)})\!+\!\displaystyle \limsup_{T

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement: As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:jumps}, we concentrate on ($\ori{\mbox{\rm a}}$) and ($\ori{\mbox{\rm b}}$). ($\ori{\mbox{\rm a}}$) This is a consequence of Lemma~\ref{l:jumps}($\ori{\mbox{\rm a}}$), since $\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})=\ori{v}(t)$ and, by virtue of \eq{e:ttos}, $\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t)})=\ori{v}(t-0)$. ($\ori{\mbox{\rm b}}$) For every $s\in T_{(t,+\infty)}$, the additivity of $\riV$ implies \begin{equation*} \riV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})=\ori{v}(s)-\ori{v}(t)+\riV(F,T_{[s,+\infty)}). \end{equation*} Passing to the limit as $T\ni s\to t+0$, we get: by Lemma~\ref{l:jumps}($\ori{\mbox{\rm b}}$), \begin{equation*} \ori{v}(s)-\ori{v}(t)\to\ori{v}(t+0)-\ori{v}(t)=\limsup_{T\ni s\to t+0}e(F(t),F(s)), \end{equation*} and by \eq{e:ttoi}, $\riV(F,T_{[s,+\infty)})\to\riV(F,T_{(t,+\infty)})$.
nodes.statement_short: Read $(\ori{a})$ off Lemma 2 plus the limit equality; for $(\ori{b})$ apply additivity and let $s\to t+0$.

nodes.name: $(\ori{a})$ from Lemma 2 and the limit equality
nodes.statement: ($\ori{\mbox{\rm a}}$) This is a consequence of Lemma~\ref{l:jumps}($\ori{\mbox{\rm a}}$), since $\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})=\ori{v}(t)$ and, by virtue of \eq{e:ttos}, $\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t)})=\ori{v}(t-0)$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})=\ori{v}(t)$ and $\riV(F,T_{(-\infty,t)})=\ori{v}(t-0)$.

nodes.name: $(\ori{b})$ by additivity and passage to the limit
nodes.statement: ($\ori{\mbox{\rm b}}$) For every $s\in T_{(t,+\infty)}$, the additivity of $\riV$ implies \begin{equation*} \riV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})=\ori{v}(s)-\ori{v}(t)+\riV(F,T_{[s,+\infty)}). \end{equation*} Passing to the limit as $T\ni s\to t+0$, we get: by Lemma~\ref{l:jumps}($\ori{\mbox{\rm b}}$), \begin{equation*} \ori{v}(s)-\ori{v}(t)\to\ori{v}(t+0)-\ori{v}(t)=\limsup_{T\ni s\to t+0}e(F(t),F(s)), \end{equation*} and by \eq{e:ttoi}, $\riV(F,T_{[s,+\infty)})\to\riV(F,T_{(t,+\infty)})$.
nodes.statement_short: Split $\riV(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})$ at $s$ and let $s\to t+0$ using Lemma 2$(\ori{b})$.

nodes.name: Modulus of variation $\nu_k(F,T)$
nodes.statement:
Given $F:T	o\mbox{c}(M)$, its \emph{modulus of variation/} is the nondecreasing sequence $\{
u_k(F,T)\}_{k=1}^\infty\subset[0,+\infty]$ defined by  egin{equation*} 
u_k(F,T)\!:=\sup\,\sum_{i=1}^k d_H(F(s_i),F(t_i)), \end{equation*} the supremum being taken over all collections $s_1,\dots,s_k,t_1\dots,t_k$ of $2k$ numbers from $T$ such that $s_1\le t_1\le s_2\le t_2\le\dots\le s_{k-1}\le t_{k-1}\le s_k\le t_k$. This notion was introduced in \cite{Chantur} in the context of Fourier series and extensively applied in \cite[Section~11.3]{GNW} for real valued functions. The general case of metric space valued functions was considered in \cite{JMAA05}, whence we know that $
u_k(F,T)\le
V(F,T)$ for all $k\in\Nb$, and $
u_k(F,T)	o
V(F,T)$ as $k	o\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: The nondecreasing sequence $\nu_k(F,T)$ of maximal $k$-term sums of $d_H$ over nonoverlapping pairs, increasing to $\nV(F,T)$.

nodes.name: Theorem B (pointwise selection principle in terms of the modulus of variation)
nodes.statement: Suppose $\{F_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ is a sequence of multifunctions $F_n:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ such that\/ {\rm(a)} $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\nu_k(F_n,T)=o(k)$\footnote{Equality $\mu_k=o(k)$ means as usual that $\lim_{k\to\infty}\mu_k/k=0$.}, and\/ {\rm(b)}~the closure in $\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ of the set $\{F_n(t):n\in\Nb\}$ is compact for all $t\in T$. Then $\{F_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ admits a subsequence, which converges in $\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ pointwise on $T$ to a multifunction $F:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ such that $\nu_k(F,T)=o(k)$.
nodes.statement_short: Helly-type compactness: $\limsup_n\nu_k(F_n,T)=o(k)$ plus pointwise relative compactness yields a pointwise convergent subsequence.
assumptions: Suppose $\{F_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ is a sequence of multifunctions $F_n:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ such that\/ {\rm(a)} $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\nu_k(F_n,T)=o(k)$
{\rm(b)}~the closure in $\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ of the set $\{F_n(t):n\in\Nb\}$ is compact for all $t\in T$
conclusions: Then $\{F_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ admits a subsequence, which converges in $\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ pointwise on $T$ to a multifunction $F:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ such that $\nu_k(F,T)=o(k)$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement:
We prove only item (a), item (b) being proved similarly with corresponding modifications (`to the left'). We divide the proof into six steps for clarity. Recall that $a=\inf T\in T$, and we set $b:=\sup T$. In the first four steps, we prove the theorem in the case when $t_0=a$ and $b\in T$ (so that $T\subset[t_0,b]$ is bounded), in step~5---when $t_0=a$ and $b
otin T$, and in step~6---when $t_0\!>\!a$ and $T$ is arbitrary. We employ several ideas from \cite{JMAA,MatSb}, \cite[Sections~5,~10]{Sovae}. \smallbreak {\it Step~1}. Suppose $T\subset[t_0,b]$ and $t_0,b\in T$. Since $iV(F,T)$ is finite and the variation function of $F$ to the right $\ori{v}:T	o[0,+\infty)$ is nondecreasing on~$T$, the set of its points of discontinuity on $T$ is at most countable. Denote by $T_F$ the set of points $t\in T$, which are left limit points of $T$ such that $\ori{v}(t)=\ori{v}(t-0)$. It follows that $T\setminus T_F$ is at most countable and, by Lemma~ef{l:jumps}${m(\ori{\mbox{m a}})}$,  egin{equation} \mbox{if $t\in T_F$, then $e(F(s),F(t))	o0$ as $T
i s	o t-0$.} \end{equation} Furthermore, the set $T_0$ of left isolated points of $T$ (i.e., $t\in T$ such that $T_{(t-\vep,t)}=\es$ for some $\vep>0$) is also at most countable (in fact, the intervals of ``emptiness from the left'', corresponding to different left isolated points of $T$, are disjoint, and each such interval contains a rational number). Let $Q$ denote an at most countable dense subset of $T$. We set  egin{equation*} S\!:=\{t_0,b\}\cup(T\setminus T_F)\cup T_0\cup Q \end{equation*} and note that $S\subset T$ is dense in $T$ and at most countable. With no loss of generality we may assume that $S$ is countable, say, $S=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^\infty$. Given $n\in\Nb$, the set $\pi_n=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^{n-1}\cup\{b\}$ is a partition of $T$. Ordering the points in $\pi_n$ in ascending order and denoting the resulting (ordered) partition of $T$ by $\pi_n=\{t_i^n\}_{i=0}^n$, we get  egin{eqnarray} &\mbox{$t_0=t_0^n<t_1^n<\dots<t_{n-1}^n<t_n^n=b$, \,and}&\[2pt] &\mbox{$ orall\,t\in S$ $\exists\,n_0=n_0(t)\in\Nb$ such that $t\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0$.}& \end{eqnarray} {\it Step~2}. Let us construct an approximating sequence for the desired set-valued selector of $F$. In order to do this, we need the following observation from \cite[assertion (10.2)]{Sovae}: given $X,Y\in\mbox{c}(M)$,  egin{equation} \mbox{there is $Y'\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y'\subset Y$ and $d_H(X,Y')\le e(X,Y)$.} \end{equation} In fact, it suffices to define $Y'$ as the \emph{metric projection/} of $X$ onto~$Y$:  egin{equation} Y'=\mbox{m Pr}_Y X:=\{y\in Y:\mbox{there is $x\in X$ such that $d(x,y)=d(x,Y)$}\}. \end{equation} First, given $n\in\Nb$, we define sets $Y_i^n\in\mbox{c}(M)$, $i=0,1,\dots,n$, inductively as follows. Setting $X=X_0$ and $Y=F(t_0)$ in \eq{e:proj}, we choose $Y_0:=Y'\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y_0\subset F(t_0)$ and $d_H(X_0,Y_0)\le e(X_0,F(t_0))$. We put $Y_0^n:=Y_0$ (for all $n\in\Nb$). Now, suppose $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ and the set $Y_{i-1}^n\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y_{i-1}^n\subset F(t_{i-1}^n)$ is already chosen. Then, we put $X=Y_{i-1}^n$ and $Y=F(t_i^n)$ in \eq{e:proj} and pick $Y_i^n:=Y'\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y_i^n\subset F(t_i^n)$ and  egin{equation} d_H(Y_{i-1}^n,Y_i^n)\le e(Y_{i-1}^n,F(t_i^n))\le e(F(t_{i-1}^n),F(t_i^n)). \end{equation} The approximating sequence $\Gamma_n:T	o\mbox{c}(M)$, $n\in\Nb$, is defined as a sequence of set-valued step functions of the form (cf. \cite[equation~(10.3)]{Sovae}):  egin{align} \Gamma_n(t_i^n)&:=Y_i^n\quad\mbox{for all \,$i=0,1,\dots,n;$}\[2pt] \Gamma_n(t)&:=Y_{i-1}^n\,\,\,\mbox{for all $t\in T\cap(t_{i-1}^n,t_i^n)$ and $i=1,\dots,n$} \end{align} (if $T\cap(t_{i-1}^n,t_i^n)=\es$, then $\Gamma_n$ is left undefined on $(t_{i-1}^n,t_i^n)$). Clearly,  egin{equation*} \Gamma_n(t_0)=\Gamma_n(t_0^n)=Y_0^n=Y_0\subset F(t_0)\quad \mbox{for all \,$n\in\Nb$.} \end{equation*} Moreover, by the additivity of $
V$ and \eq{e:Yin}, we have  egin{align} 
V(\Gamma_n,T)&=\sum_{i=1}^n
V(\Gamma_n,T\cap[t_{i-1}^n,t_i^n]) =\sum_{i=1}^n d_H(Y_{i-1}^n,Y_i^n)
onumber\ &\le\sum_{i=1}^n e(F(t_{i-1}^n),F(t_i^n))\leiV(F,T) \quad\mbox{for all $n\in\Nb$.} \end{align} {\it Step~3}. Let us show that $\{\Gamma_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem~ef{t:B}. By virtue of \eq{e:gn}, we get  egin{equation*} \limsup_{n	o\infty}
u_k(\Gamma_n,T)\leiV(F,T)\quad\mbox{for all \,$k\in\Nb$,} \end{equation*} and so, condition (a) in Theorem~ef{t:B} is satisfied. Now, we verify condition~(b). If $t\in S$, then, by \eq{e:noN}, there is $n_0=n_0(t)\in\Nb$ such that $t\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0$. So, for each $n\ge n_0$ there is $i=i(t,n)\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}$ such that $t=t_i^n$. The definition of $\Gamma_n$ implies  egin{equation} \Gamma_n(t)=\Gamma_n(t_i^n)=Y_i^n\subset F(t_i^n)=F(t)\quad \mbox{for all \,$n\ge n_0$.} \end{equation} In other words, $\{\Gamma_n(t)\}_{n=n_0}^\infty\subset\mbox{c}(F(t))$. Since $F(t)$ is a compact subset of $M$, it follows from \cite[II.1.4]{CV} that $\mbox{c}(F(t))$ is a compact subset of $\mbox{c}(M)$, which implies the desired property for $\{F_n(t)\}_{n=1}^\infty$. Suppose now that $t\in T\setminus S$. We have $t\in T_F\cap(t_0,b)$, i.e., by \eq{e:FsFt},  egin{equation} e(F(s),F(t))	o0\quad\mbox{as}\quad T_{(t_0,b)}
i s	o t-0, \end{equation} where $t$ is a left limit point of $T$, and so, there is a sequence $	au_k\in T$, $	au_k<t$, $k\in\Nb$, such that $	au_k	o t$ as $k	o\infty$. Since $S$ is dense in $T$, given $k\in\Nb$, there is $s_k\in S$ such that $|s_k-	au_k|<t-	au_k$, which implies $s_k<t$, and $s_k	o t$ as $k	o\infty$. From \eq{e:noN}, for each $k\in\Nb$ choose a number $n_0(k)\in\Nb$ (depending also on~$t$) such that $s_k\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0(k)$. We may assume (arguing inductively) that the sequence $\{n_0(k)\}_{k=1}^\infty$ is strictly increasing. Given $k\in\Nb$ and $n\ge n_0(k)$, since $s_k\in\pi_n$, there is a number $j(k,n)\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ such that $s_k=t_{j(k,n)}^n$ and, since $s_k<t$, there is (unique) $i(k,n)\in\{j(k,n),\dots,n-1\}$ such that  egin{equation} s_k=t_{j(k,n)}^n\le t_{i(k,n)}^n<t<t_{i(k,n)+1}^n. \end{equation} By \eq{e:4+}, \eq{e:re}, and \eq{e:ijkn}, we find  egin{equation} \Gamma_n(t)=Y_{i(k,n)}^n\subset F(t_{i(k,n)}^n)\quad\mbox{for all \,$k\in\Nb$ \,and \,$n\ge n_0(k)$.} \end{equation} Setting $n:=n_0(k)$ and $p_k:=t_{i(k,n_0(k))}^{n_0(k)}$ in \eq{e:Fikn}, we have $\Gamma_{n_0(k)}(t)\subset F(p_k)$ for all $k\in\Nb$, where, by virtue of \eq{e:ijkn} and property $s_k	o t$ as $k	o\infty$,  egin{equation} \mbox{$p_k<t$ \,and \,$p_k	o t$ \,as \,$k	o\infty$.} \end{equation} Applying \eq{e:proj}, for each $k\in\Nb$ pick $Y_k(t)\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y_k(t)\subset F(t)$ and  egin{equation} d_H(\Gamma_{n_0(k)},Y_k(t))\le e(\Gamma_{n_0(k)},F(t))\le e(F(p_k),F(t)). \end{equation} It follows from \eq{e:*7} and \eq{e:pkt} that the right-hand side in \eq{e:Gok} tends to zero as $k	o\infty$. By the compactness of $\mbox{c}(F(t))$, we may assume (passing to a subsequence of $\{Y_k(t)\}_{k=1}^\infty$ if necessary) that $d_H(Y_k(t),Y(t))	o0$ as $k	o\infty$ for some $Y(t)\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y(t)\subset F(t)$. Thus,  egin{equation*} d_H(\Gamma_{n_0(k)}(t),Y(t))\!\le\! d_H(\Gamma_{n_0(k)}(t),Y_k(t)) \!+\!d_H(Y_k(t),Y(t))\!	o\!0\quad\mbox{as \,$k\!	o\!\infty$,} \end{equation*} and so, (a subsequence of) the subsequence $\{\Gamma_{n_0(k)}\}_{k=1}^\infty$ of $\{\Gamma_n(t)\}_{n=1}^\infty$ converges in $\mbox{c}(M)$. This finishes the proof of compactness of $\ov{\{\Gamma_n(t)\}_{n=1}^\infty}$ (the closure being taken in $\mbox{c}(M)$). \smallbreak {\it Step~4}. By Theorem~ef{t:B}, there are a subsequence of $\{\Gamma_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$, which we denote by $\{\Gamma_{l(n)}\}_{n=1}^\infty$ with strictly increasing $l:\Nb	o\Nb$, and a multifunction $\Gamma:T	o\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $d_H(\Gamma_{l(n)}(t),\Gamma(t))	o0$ as $n	o\infty$ for all $t\in T$. Let us show that $\Gamma$ is a set-valued selector of $F$ on $T$. It is clear from \eq{e:4+} and \eq{e:op} that $\Gamma(t_0)=Y_0\subset F(t_0)$, and so (cf. Step~2),  egin{equation} d_H(X_0,\Gamma(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0)). \end{equation} If $t\in S$, \eq{e:noN} implies $t\in\pi_n$ for some $n_0=n_0(t)\in\Nb$ and all $n\ge n_0$. Since $l(n)\ge l(n_0)\ge n_0$ for $n\ge n_0$, it follows from \eq{e:Gat} that $\Gamma_{l(n)}(t)\subset F(t)$, and so (cf.\ properties (a) and (b) of $e$ in Section~ef{s:mr}),  egin{align*} e(\Gamma(t),F(t))&\le e(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{l(n)}(t)) +e(\Gamma_{l(n)}(t),F(t)) \[2pt] &=e(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{l(n)}(t))\le d_H(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{l(n)}(t)) 	o0\quad\mbox{as \,$n	o\infty$.} \end{align*} This gives $e(\Gamma(t),F(t))=0$ implying $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$. Now suppose that $t\in T\setminus S$. Given $k\in\Nb$, let $n_0(k)$ be the number (also depending on $t$) from Step~3 such that $s_k\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0(k)$. Hence, assertions \eq{e:ijkn} and \eq{e:Fikn} still hold. Setting $n=N(k):=l(n_0(k))\ge n_0(k)$ and $q_k:=t_{i(k,N(k))}^{N(k)}$ in \eq{e:ijkn} and \eq{e:Fikn}, we find $\Gamma_{N(k)}\subset F(q_k)$, where $q_k<t$, and $q_k	o t$ as $k	o\infty$. For each $k\in\Nb$, thanks to \eq{e:proj}, let $Z_k(t)\in\mbox{c}(M)$ be such that $Z_k(t)\subset F(t)$ and  egin{equation*} d_H(\Gamma_{N(k)}(t),Z_k(t))\le e(\Gamma_{N(k)}(t),F(t))\le e(F(q_k),F(t)). \end{equation*} Noting that $e(Z_k(t),F(t))=0$, we get  egin{equation*} e(\Gamma(t),F(t))\le e(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{N(k)}(t)) +e(\Gamma_{N(k)}(t),Z_k(t))+e(Z_k(t),F(t)) \end{equation*} with the right-hand side tending to zero as $n\!	o\!\infty$. Hence \mbox{$e(\Gamma(t),F(t))\!=\!0$}, and so, $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$. Thus, we have shown that $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$ for all $t\in T$. The lower semicontinuity of $
V$ and \eq{e:gn} imply  egin{equation*} 
V(\Gamma,T)\le\liminf_{n	o\infty}
V(\Gamma_{l(n)},T)\leiV(F,T). \end{equation*} Since $T_{[a,t_0)}\!=\!\es$ (recall that $t_0\!=\!a$), $T_{[t_0,+\infty)}\!=\!T_{[t_0,b]}\!=\!T$, and \mbox{$J_a(\Gamma,t_0)\!=\!0$}, this proves Theorem~ef{t:BV}(a) in the case when $t_0=a$ and $b=\sup T\in T$. \smallbreak {\it Remark}. Note that if $X_0\subset F(t_0)$, we have, by \eq{e:Xo}, $\Gamma(t_0)=X_0$. \smallbreak {\it Step~5}. Suppose $t_0=a$ and $b=\sup T

Noting that $iV(F,T_{[t_0,t_1]})\leiV(F,T)<+\infty$ and applying Steps 1--4 to $F$ on $T_{[t_0,t_1]}$, we get a set-valued selector $\Gamma_0:T_{[t_0,t_1]}	o\mbox{c}(M)$ of $F$ on $T_{[t_0,t_1]}$ such that  egin{equation*} d_H(X_0,\Gamma_0(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0))\quad\mbox{and}\quad

nodes.statement_short: Six-step construction: build step-multifunction approximants $\Gamma_n$ by iterated metric projections along a dense countable partition mesh, extract a pointwise limit via Theorem B, and patch the pieces for unbounded $T$ and for $t_0>a$.

nodes.name: Step 1: choice of a dense countable set $S$ and partitions $\pi_n$
nodes.statement: {\it Step~1}. Suppose $T\subset[t_0,b]$ and $t_0,b\in T$. Since $\riV(F,T)$ is finite and the variation function of $F$ to the right $\ori{v}:T\to[0,+\infty)$ is nondecreasing on~$T$, the set of its points of discontinuity on $T$ is at most countable. Denote by $T_F$ the set of points $t\in T$, which are left limit points of $T$ such that $\ori{v}(t)=\ori{v}(t-0)$. It follows that $T\setminus T_F$ is at most countable and, by Lemma~\ref{l:jumps}${\rm(\ori{\mbox{\rm a}})}$, \begin{equation} \mbox{if $t\in T_F$, then $e(F(s),F(t))\to0$ as $T\ni s\to t-0$.} \end{equation} Furthermore, the set $T_0$ of left isolated points of $T$ (i.e., $t\in T$ such that $T_{(t-\vep,t)}=\es$ for some $\vep>0$) is also at most countable (in fact, the intervals of ``emptiness from the left'', corresponding to different left isolated points of $T$, are disjoint, and each such interval contains a rational number). Let $Q$ denote an at most countable dense subset of $T$. We set \begin{equation*} S\!:=\{t_0,b\}\cup(T\setminus T_F)\cup T_0\cup Q \end{equation*} and note that $S\subset T$ is dense in $T$ and at most countable. With no loss of generality we may assume that $S$ is countable, say, $S=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^\infty$. Given $n\in\Nb$, the set $\pi_n=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^{n-1}\cup\{b\}$ is a partition of $T$. Ordering the points in $\pi_n$ in ascending order and denoting the resulting (ordered) partition of $T$ by $\pi_n=\{t_i^n\}_{i=0}^n$, we get \begin{eqnarray} &\mbox{$t_0=t_0^n<t_1^n<\dots<t_{n-1}^n<t_n^n=b$, \,and}&\\[2pt] &\mbox{$\forall\,t\in S$ $\exists\,n_0=n_0(t)\in\Nb$ such that $t\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0$.}& \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Collect the at most countably many bad points plus a dense set into $S$ and build exhausting ordered partitions $\pi_n$.

nodes.name: Step 2: construction of the approximating step multifunctions $\Gamma_n$
nodes.statement: {\it Step~2}. Let us construct an approximating sequence for the desired set-valued selector of $F$. In order to do this, we need the following observation from \cite[assertion (10.2)]{Sovae}: given $X,Y\in\mbox{c}(M)$, \begin{equation} \mbox{there is $Y'\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y'\subset Y$ and $d_H(X,Y')\le e(X,Y)$.} \end{equation} In fact, it suffices to define $Y'$ as the \emph{metric projection\/} of $X$ onto~$Y$: \begin{equation} Y'=\mbox{\rm Pr}_Y X:=\{y\in Y:\mbox{there is $x\in X$ such that $d(x,y)=d(x,Y)$}\}. \end{equation} First, given $n\in\Nb$, we define sets $Y_i^n\in\mbox{c}(M)$, $i=0,1,\dots,n$, inductively as follows. Setting $X=X_0$ and $Y=F(t_0)$ in \eq{e:proj}, we choose $Y_0:=Y'\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y_0\subset F(t_0)$ and $d_H(X_0,Y_0)\le e(X_0,F(t_0))$. We put $Y_0^n:=Y_0$ (for all $n\in\Nb$). Now, suppose $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ and the set $Y_{i-1}^n\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y_{i-1}^n\subset F(t_{i-1}^n)$ is already chosen. Then, we put $X=Y_{i-1}^n$ and $Y=F(t_i^n)$ in \eq{e:proj} and pick $Y_i^n:=Y'\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y_i^n\subset F(t_i^n)$ and \begin{equation} d_H(Y_{i-1}^n,Y_i^n)\le e(Y_{i-1}^n,F(t_i^n))\le e(F(t_{i-1}^n),F(t_i^n)). \end{equation} The approximating sequence $\Gamma_n:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$, $n\in\Nb$, is defined as a sequence of set-valued step functions of the form (cf. \cite[equation~(10.3)]{Sovae}): \begin{align} \Gamma_n(t_i^n)&:=Y_i^n\quad\mbox{for all \,$i=0,1,\dots,n;$}\\[2pt] \Gamma_n(t)&:=Y_{i-1}^n\,\,\,\mbox{for all $t\in T\cap(t_{i-1}^n,t_i^n)$ and $i=1,\dots,n$} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Iterate the metric-projection observation along $\pi_n$ to build $\Gamma_n$ with $\nV(\Gamma_n,T)\le\riV(F,T)$.

nodes.name: Step 3: verification of the hypotheses of Theorem B
nodes.statement: {\it Step~3}. Let us show that $\{\Gamma_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{t:B}. By virtue of \eq{e:gn}, we get \begin{equation*} \limsup_{n\to\infty}\nu_k(\Gamma_n,T)\le\riV(F,T)\quad\mbox{for all \,$k\in\Nb$,} \end{equation*} and so, condition (a) in Theorem~\ref{t:B} is satisfied. Now, we verify condition~(b). If $t\in S$, then, by \eq{e:noN}, there is $n_0=n_0(t)\in\Nb$ such that $t\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0$. So, for each $n\ge n_0$ there is $i=i(t,n)\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}$ such that $t=t_i^n$. The definition of $\Gamma_n$ implies \begin{equation} \Gamma_n(t)=\Gamma_n(t_i^n)=Y_i^n\subset F(t_i^n)=F(t)\quad \mbox{for all \,$n\ge n_0$.} \end{equation} In other words, $\{\Gamma_n(t)\}_{n=n_0}^\infty\subset\mbox{c}(F(t))$. Since $F(t)$ is a compact subset of $M$, it follows from \cite[II.1.4]{CV} that $\mbox{c}(F(t))$ is a compact subset of $\mbox{c}(M)$, which implies the desired property for $\{F_n(t)\}_{n=1}^\infty$. Suppose now that $t\in T\setminus S$. We have $t\in T_F\cap(t_0,b)$, i.e., by \eq{e:FsFt}, \begin{equation} e(F(s),F(t))\to0\quad\mbox{as}\quad T_{(t_0,b)}\ni s\to t-0, \end{equation} where $t$ is a left limit point of $T$, and so, there is a sequence $\tau_k\in T$, $\tau_k<t$, $k\in\Nb$, such that $\tau_k\to t$ as $k\to\infty$. Since $S$ is dense in $T$, given $k\in\Nb$, there is $s_k\in S$ such that $|s_k-\tau_k|<t-\tau_k$, which implies $s_k<t$, and $s_k\to t$ as $k\to\infty$. From \eq{e:noN}, for each $k\in\Nb$ choose a number $n_0(k)\in\Nb$ (depending also on~$t$) such that $s_k\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0(k)$. We may assume (arguing inductively) that the sequence $\{n_0(k)\}_{k=1}^\infty$ is strictly increasing. Given $k\in\Nb$ and $n\ge n_0(k)$, since $s_k\in\pi_n$, there is a number $j(k,n)\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ such that $s_k=t_{j(k,n)}^n$ and, since $s_k<t$, there is (unique) $i(k,n)\in\{j(k,n),\dots,n-1\}$ such that \begin{equation} s_k=t_{j(k,n)}^n\le t_{i(k,n)}^n<t<t_{i(k,n)+1}^n. \end{equation} By \eq{e:4+}, \eq{e:re}, and \eq{e:ijkn}, we find \begin{equation} \Gamma_n(t)=Y_{i(k,n)}^n\subset F(t_{i(k,n)}^n)\quad\mbox{for all \,$k\in\Nb$ \,and \,$n\ge n_0(k)$.} \end{equation} Setting $n:=n_0(k)$ and $p_k:=t_{i(k,n_0(k))}^{n_0(k)}$ in \eq{e:Fikn}, we have $\Gamma_{n_0(k)}(t)\subset F(p_k)$ for all $k\in\Nb$, where, by virtue of \eq{e:ijkn} and property $s_k\to t$ as $k\to\infty$, \begin{equation} \mbox{$p_k<t$ \,and \,$p_k\to t$ \,as \,$k\to\infty$.} \end{equation} Applying \eq{e:proj}, for each $k\in\Nb$ pick $Y_k(t)\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y_k(t)\subset F(t)$ and \begin{equation} d_H(\Gamma_{n_0(k)},Y_k(t))\le e(\Gamma_{n_0(k)},F(t))\le e(F(p_k),F(t)). \end{equation} It follows from \eq{e:*7} and \eq{e:pkt} that the right-hand side in \eq{e:Gok} tends to zero as $k\to\infty$. By the compactness of $\mbox{c}(F(t))$, we may assume (passing to a subsequence of $\{Y_k(t)\}_{k=1}^\infty$ if necessary) that $d_H(Y_k(t),Y(t))\to0$ as $k\to\infty$ for some $Y(t)\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y(t)\subset F(t)$. Thus, \begin{equation*} d_H(\Gamma_{n_0(k)}(t),Y(t))\!\le\! d_H(\Gamma_{n_0(k)}(t),Y_k(t)) \!+\!d_H(Y_k(t),Y(t))\!\to\!0\quad\mbox{as \,$k\!\to\!\infty$,} \end{equation*} and so, (a subsequence of) the subsequence $\{\Gamma_{n_0(k)}\}_{k=1}^\infty$ of $\{\Gamma_n(t)\}_{n=1}^\infty$ converges in $\mbox{c}(M)$. This finishes the proof of compactness of $\ov{\{\Gamma_n(t)\}_{n=1}^\infty}$ (the closure being taken in $\mbox{c}(M)$).

nodes.name: Existence of a compact subset realising the excess (metric-projection observation)
nodes.statement: we need the following observation from \cite[assertion (10.2)]{Sovae}: given $X,Y\in\mbox{c}(M)$, \begin{equation} \mbox{there is $Y'\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y'\subset Y$ and $d_H(X,Y')\le e(X,Y)$.} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For compact $X,Y$ there is a compact $Y'\subset Y$ with $d_H(X,Y')\le e(X,Y)$.
assumptions: given $X,Y\in\mbox{c}(M)$
conclusions: there is $Y'\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y'\subset Y$ and $d_H(X,Y')\le e(X,Y)$.

nodes.name: Metric projection $\mbox{\rm Pr}_Y X$
nodes.statement: In fact, it suffices to define $Y'$ as the \emph{metric projection\/} of $X$ onto~$Y$: \begin{equation} Y'=\mbox{\rm Pr}_Y X:=\{y\in Y:\mbox{there is $x\in X$ such that $d(x,y)=d(x,Y)$}\}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof (of Theorem A) from Theorem 1
nodes.statement:
Setting $T_+=T_{[t_0,+\infty)}$ and $T_-=T_{(-\infty,t_0]}$, we have  egin{equation*} iV(F,T_+)\le
V(F,T_+)\le
V(F,T)\quad\mbox{and}\quad \leV(F,T_-)\le
V(F,T_-)\le
V(F,T). \end{equation*} Noting that $t_0\in T_+\cap T_-$ and applying Theorem~ef{t:BV}(a) to $F$ on $T_+$ and Theorem~ef{t:BV}(b) to $F$ on $T_-$, we obtain a set-valued selector $\Gamma_+:T_+	o\mbox{c}(M)$ of $F$ on $T_+$ and a set-valued selector $\Gamma_-:T_-	o\mbox{c}(M)$ of $F$ on $T_-$ such that  egin{eqnarray*} &d_H(X_0,\Gamma_+(t_0))\!\le\! e(X_0,F(t_0))\quad\!\mbox{and}\quad\! 
V(\Gamma_+,T_+)\!\le\!iV(F,T_+),&\[2pt] &d_H(\Gamma_+(t_0),\Gamma_-(t_0))\!\le\! e(\Gamma_+(t_0),F(t_0))\!=\!0\quad\! \mbox{and}\!\quad
V(\Gamma_-,T_-)\!\le\!\leV(F,T_-).& \end{eqnarray*} Noting that $\Gamma_-(t_0)=\Gamma_+(t_0)$, we set $\Gamma(t):=\Gamma_+(t)$ if $t\in T_+$, and $\Gamma(t):=\Gamma_-(t)$ if $t\in T_-\setminus\{t_0\}$. Clearly, $\Gamma:T	o\mbox{c}(M)$ is a set-valued selector of $F$ on $T$, $d_H(X_0,\Gamma(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0))$ and, by the additivity of~$
V$,  egin{align} 
V(\Gamma,T)&=
V(\Gamma,T_+)+
V(\Gamma,T_-)= 
V(\Gamma_+,T_+)+
V(\Gamma_-,T_-)
onumber\[1pt] &\leiV(F,T_+)+\leV(F,T_-) \[2pt] &\le
V(F,T_+)+
V(F,T_-)=
V(F,T). 
onumber \end{align} This finishes the proof of Theorem~ef{t:A}. Note that we have shown a little bit more: inequality \eq{RR} holds provided $iV(F,T_+)$ and $\leV(F,T_-)$ are finite.
nodes.statement_short: Split $T$ at $t_0$, apply Theorem 1(a) to the right half and Theorem 1(b) to the left half, and glue the two selectors, which agree at $t_0$.

nodes.name: Bound the one-sided variations by $\nV(F,T)$
nodes.statement:
Setting $T_+=T_{[t_0,+\infty)}$ and $T_-=T_{(-\infty,t_0]}$, we have  egin{equation*} iV(F,T_+)\le
V(F,T_+)\le
V(F,T)\quad\mbox{and}\quad \leV(F,T_-)\le
V(F,T_-)\le
V(F,T). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: On the two halves the directional variations are dominated by $\nV(F,T)$.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 1(a) and 1(b) on the two halves
nodes.statement: Noting that $t_0\in T_+\cap T_-$ and applying Theorem~\ref{t:BV}(a) to $F$ on $T_+$ and Theorem~\ref{t:BV}(b) to $F$ on $T_-$, we obtain a set-valued selector $\Gamma_+:T_+\to\mbox{c}(M)$ of $F$ on $T_+$ and a set-valued selector $\Gamma_-:T_-\to\mbox{c}(M)$ of $F$ on $T_-$ such that \begin{eqnarray*} &d_H(X_0,\Gamma_+(t_0))\!\le\! e(X_0,F(t_0))\quad\!\mbox{and}\quad\! \nV(\Gamma_+,T_+)\!\le\!\riV(F,T_+),&\\[2pt] &d_H(\Gamma_+(t_0),\Gamma_-(t_0))\!\le\! e(\Gamma_+(t_0),F(t_0))\!=\!0\quad\! \mbox{and}\!\quad\nV(\Gamma_-,T_-)\!\le\!\leV(F,T_-).& \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Get selectors $\Gamma_+$ on $T_+$ and $\Gamma_-$ on $T_-$ with matching value at $t_0$.

Noting that $\Gamma_-(t_0)=\Gamma_+(t_0)$, we set $\Gamma(t):=\Gamma_+(t)$ if $t\in T_+$, and $\Gamma(t):=\Gamma_-(t)$ if $t\in T_-\setminus\{t_0\}$. Clearly, $\Gamma:T	o\mbox{c}(M)$ is a set-valued selector of $F$ on $T$, $d_H(X_0,\Gamma(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0))$ and, by the additivity of~$
V$,  egin{align} 
V(\Gamma,T)&=
V(\Gamma,T_+)+
V(\Gamma,T_-)= 
V(\Gamma_+,T_+)+
V(\Gamma_-,T_-)
onumber\[1pt] &\leiV(F,T_+)+\leV(F,T_-) \[2pt] &\le
V(F,T_+)+
V(F,T_-)=
V(F,T). 
onumber \end{align} This finishes the proof of Theorem~ef{t:A}. Note that we have shown a little bit more: inequality \eq{RR} holds provided $iV(F,T_+)$ and $\leV(F,T_-)$ are finite.

Additivity of $
V$ gives $

nodes.name: Single-valued selectors: pick one element of the metric projection
nodes.statement: If $X_0=\{x_0\}\subset M$, a (single-valued) selector of bounded var\-i\-a\-tion $\Gamma:T\!\to\! M$ of $F$ on $T$ may be chosen such that \mbox{$d(x_0,\Gamma(t_0))\!\le\! d(x_0,F(t_0))$} and satisfying the rest of assertions in (a) and (b) of Theorem~\ref{t:BV} (if we replace $d_H$ by $d$ everywhere). In order to see this, it suffices to pick only one element in the corresponding metric projection. So (cf. Step~2 in the proof of Theorem~\ref{t:BV}), choose $y_0\in F(t_0)$ such that $d(x_0,y_0)=d(x_0,F(t_0))$, set $y_0^n:=y_0$, and if $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ and elements $y_{i-1}^n\in F(t_{i-1}^n)$ are already chosen, pick \mbox{$y_i^n\in F(t_i^n)$} such that $d(y_{i-1}^n,y_i^n)=d(y_{i-1}^n,F(t_i^n))$. Define $\Gamma_n:T\to M$ (as in \eq{e:4+} and \eq{e:re}) by $\Gamma_n(t_i^n):=y_i^n$ for $i=0,1,\dots,n$, and $\Gamma_n(t):=y_{i-1}^n$ if $t\in T\cap(t_{i-1}^n,t_i^n)$ and $i=1,\dots,n$. It remains to note (for $T\subset[t_0,b]$) that \begin{align*} \nV(\Gamma_n,T)&=\nV(\Gamma_n,T\cap[t_{i-1}^n,t_i^n]) =\sum_{i=1}^n d(y_{i-1}^n,y_i^n)\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^n d(y_{i-1}^n,F(t_i^n))\le\sum_{i=1}^n e(F(t_{i-1}^n),F(t_i^n)) \le\riV(F,T). \end{align*} In this way, Theorem~\ref{t:BV} above is a generalization of \cite[Theorem~1]{JMAA07}, treating the existence of single-valued selectors on (connected) intervals $T\subset\Rb$.
nodes.statement_short: Choosing a single nearest point at each stage yields the single-valued version of Theorem 1, generalising Chistyakov-Repovš 2007.

nodes.name: The ambient space $M=\ell_1(\Nb;\mathbb{B})$ and the unit vectors $u_n$
nodes.statement: Let $(\mathbb{B},|\cdot|)$ be a Banach space with norm $|\cdot|$ (e.g., $\mathbb{B}=\Rb$), $\mathbb{B}^\Nb$ be the set of all sequences $x:\Nb\to\mathbb{B}$, and $M=\ell_1(\Nb;\mathbb{B})$ be the (infinite-dimensional) Banach space of all \emph{summable\/} sequences $x\in\mathbb{B}^\Nb$ equipped with the norm $\|x\|:=\sum_{i=1}^\infty|x(i)|<+\infty$ and, hence, metric $d(x,y):=\|x-y\|$ for $x,y\in M$. Fix $u\in\mathbb{B}$ with $|u|=1$ (e.g., $u=1$ in $\Rb$) and, for every $n\in\Nb$, denote by $u_n$ the unit vector in $M$ defined as usual by $u_n(i)=0$ if $i\ne n$, and $u_n(n)=u$.
nodes.statement_short: All counterexamples live in the summable-sequence space $\ell_1(\Nb;\mathbb{B})$ with its coordinate unit vectors $u_n$.
nodes.genus: the (infinite-dimensional) Banach space of all \emph{summable\/} sequences $x\in\mathbb{B}^\Nb$

nodes.name: Example 1 (bounded closed but noncompact values: no selector satisfying the estimates)
nodes.statement_short: With $F(0)=X$, $F(t)=Y$ merely bounded closed, $\riV(F,T)=2$ but every selector violates the variation and initial-value estimates because $\mbox{Pr}_YX_0=\es$.

nodes.name: Example 2 (failure at a single noncompact value)
nodes.statement_short: Even one bounded-closed noncompact value $F(1)=Y$ destroys the estimates of Theorem 1, while part (b) still holds with $\Gamma(1)=X_0$.

nodes.name: Example 3 (finite right variation with infinite left variation)
nodes.statement: Making use of an idea from \cite[Example~3.1]{JMAA07}, here we present an example of a multifunction $F:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ with $T:=[0,1]$ such that $\riV(F,T)<+\infty$ and $\leV(F,T)=+\infty$ (thus, Theorem~\ref{t:BV}(a) is applicable to $F$, whereas Theorem~\ref{t:A} is not). Let $N\in\Nb$ and $\{\alpha_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\subset(0,+\infty)$ be a decreasing sequence such that \begin{equation} \lim_{n\to\infty}\alpha_n=0\quad\mbox{and}\quad \sum_{n=1}^\infty\alpha_{nN}=+\infty \end{equation} (e.g., $\alpha_n=1/n$). Given $n\in\Nb$, we set \begin{equation*} X_n:=\{0\}\cup\{\alpha_iu_i:1\le i\le nN\},\quad\mbox{and}\quad X_\infty:=\{0\}\cup\{\alpha_iu_i:i\in\Nb\}. \end{equation*} Clearly, $X_n\in\mbox{c}(M)$ for all $n\in\Nb$ and, by the first assumption in \eq{e:Alph}, the set $X_\infty$ is compact as well. Let $\{\tau_n\}_{n=0}^\infty\subset[0,1)$ be a strictly increasing sequence such that $\tau_0=0$ and $\lim_{n\to\infty}\tau_n=1$. Define $F:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ by the rule: \begin{equation*} \mbox{$F(t):=X_n$ \,if\, $\tau_{n-1}\le t<\tau_n$ for all $n\in\Nb$, \,and\, $F(1):=X_\infty$.} \end{equation*} Since $X_n\subset X_{n+1}\subset X_\infty$ for all $n\in\Nb$, $F$ is nondecreasing on $T$ (Section~\ref{ss:mon}), and so, $\riV(F,T)=0$. In order to see that $\leV(F,T)=+\infty$, given $m\in\Nb$, $m\ge2$, and partition $\pi_m=\{\tau_n\}_{n=0}^{m-1}\cup\{1\}$ of $T=[0,1]$, we find \begin{align} \leV(F,T)&\ge\sum_{n=1}^{m-1}e(F(\tau_n),F(\tau_{n-1}))+e(F(1),F(\tau_{m-1})) \nonumber\\ &=\sum_{n=1}^{m-1}e(X_{n+1},X_n)+e(X_\infty,X_m), \end{align} where \begin{equation*} e(X_{n+1},X_n)=\sup_{nN+1\le k\le(n+1)N}\Bigl(|\alpha_k|+ \inf_{1\le i\le nN}|\alpha_i|\Bigr)=\alpha_{nN+1}+\alpha_{nN} \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} e(X_\infty,X_m)=\sup_{k\ge mN+1}\Bigl(|\alpha_k|+ \inf_{1\le i\le mN}|\alpha_i|\Bigr)=\alpha_{mN+1}+\alpha_{mN}. \end{equation*} It follows that the quantity \eq{e:rhs} is equal to \begin{equation*} \sum_{n=1}^m\alpha_{nN+1}+\sum_{n=1}^m\alpha_{nN}\to+\infty\quad \mbox{as}\quad m\to\infty. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: A nondecreasing compact-valued $F$ on $[0,1]$ with $\riV(F,T)=0$ and $\leV(F,T)=+\infty$, so Theorem 1(a) applies but Theorem A does not.

nodes.name: Example 4 (necessity of $t_0=a$ and of the jump term $J_a$)
nodes.statement:
(a) By Theorem~ef{t:BV}(a), given $X_0\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $X_0\subset X_1=F(0)$, multifunction $F$ from Example~ef{ex3} has a constant set-valued selector $\Gamma:T	o\mbox{c}(M)$ satisfying $\Gamma(0)=X_0$ and $
V(\Gamma,T)\leiV(F,T)=0$. However, if $0<t_0\le1$ and $X_0\subset F(t_0)$, there may be no set-valued selector $\Gamma$ of $F$ on $T$ such that $\Gamma(t_0)=X_0$ and $
V(\Gamma,T)\leiV(F,T)$. In fact, let $t_0=	au_n$ for some $n\in\Nb$ (cf. Example~ef{ex3}), so that $F(t_0)=F(	au_n)=X_{n+1}$. Suppose now that $X_0\subset X_{n+1}\setminus X_1\subset F(t_0)$, $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$ for all $t\in T$, and $\Gamma(t_0)=X_0$. Since $\Gamma(0)\subset F(0)=X_1$, we have $\alpha_iu_i\in\Gamma(0)$ for some $1\le i\le N$, or $0\in\Gamma(0)$ (i.e., possibly, $\alpha_i=0$), and so,  egin{align} 
V(\Gamma,T)&\ge d_H(\Gamma(t_0),\Gamma(0))=d_H(X_0,\Gamma(0)) \ge e(\Gamma(0),X_0)
onumber\[3pt] &\ge d(\alpha_iu_i,X_0)\ge d(\alpha_iu_i,X_{n+1}\setminus X_1)
onumber\[2pt] &=\min_{N+1\le k\le (n+1)N}(\alpha_i+\alpha_k)\ge\alpha_{(n+1)N} >0=iV(F,T). \end{align} (b) If $t_0>a=\inf T$ and $\Gamma(t_0)=X_0$, inequality $
V(\Gamma,T_{[a,t_0)})\leiV(F,T_{[a,t_0)})$ in Theorem~ef{t:BV}(a) cannot in general be replaced by $
V(\Gamma,T_{[a,t_0]})\leiV(F,T_{[a,t_0]})$. This can be seen from Example~ef{ex4} and \eq{e:519}:  egin{equation*} 
V(\Gamma,[0,t_0])\ge d_H(\Gamma(t_0),\Gamma(0))\ge\dots\ge \alpha_{(n+1)N}>0=iV(F,[0,t_0]). \end{equation*} This observation also makes it explicit that the ``jump'' $J_a(\Gamma,t_0)$ is essential in the left-hand side of \eq{e:s1t0}.
nodes.statement_short: For $t_0>0$ no selector meets $\nV(\Gamma,T)\le\riV(F,T)$, showing the half-open interval and the jump $J_a(\Gamma,t_0)$ in Theorem 1(a) are essential.

nodes.name: Example 5 (image not totally bounded under finite right variation)
nodes.statement: This example is designed for Remark~\ref{p:7}. Let $T:=[1,+\infty)$ and $F:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ be given by $F(t)\!:=\!X_n$ if $n\in\Nb$ and $n\le t<n+1$, where $X_n\!:=\!\{u_i:1\le i\le n\}$. We have $X_n\in\mbox{c}(M)$, and $F(s)\subset F(t)$ for all $1\le s\le t<+\infty$, and so, $\riV(F,T)=0$. The image \mbox{$F(T)=\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty X_n=\{u_i:i\in\Nb\}$} is bounded in $M$, but \emph{not\/} totally bounded (i.e., cannot be covered by a finite number of balls of arbitrarily small radius). Note that $\leV(F,T)=+\infty$ (consider a partition $1<2<\dots<m-1<m$ of $T$ with arbitrary $m\in\Nb$ and observe that $e(X_{n+1},X_n)=2$ for all $n\in\Nb$). This example is easily adapted to the case when $F$ maps $[a,b)$ or $[a,b]$ into~$\mbox{c}(M)$.
nodes.statement_short: $F(t)=\{u_i:i\le n\}$ on $[1,+\infty)$ has $\riV(F,T)=0$ yet $F(T)$ is bounded but not totally bounded.

nodes.name: Theorem 2 (parametrized contraction theorem for the functional inclusion $X(t)\subset F(t,X(t))$)
nodes.statement: Suppose a multifunction $F:T\!\times\!\mbox{\rm c}(M)\!\to\!\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ is such that\/{\rm:} \begin{itemize} \item[{\rm(a)}] there is a nondecreasing bounded function $\varphi:T\to\Rb$ such that \begin{equation*} \mbox{$\!\!\!e(F(s,X),F(t,X))\le\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)$ for all $s,t\in T$, $s\le T$, and $X\in\mbox{\rm c}(M);$} \end{equation*} \item[{\rm(b)}] there is a number $0\le\mu<1$ such that \begin{equation*} \mbox{$e(F(t,X),F(t,Y))\le\mu d_H(X,Y)$ for all $t\in T$ and $X,Y\in\mbox{\rm c}(M);$} \end{equation*} \item[{\rm(c)}] there is a multifunction $K:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ such that \begin{equation*} \mbox{$F(t,X)\subset K(t)$ for all $t\in T$ and $X\in\mbox{\rm c}(M)$.} \end{equation*} \end{itemize} If $t_0:=\inf T\in T$ and $X_0\in\mbox{\rm c}(M)$, then there is $X:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ such that\\[3pt] {\rm(i)}~$\nV(X,T)\le\nV(\varphi,T)/(1-\mu)<+\infty;$ {\rm(ii)}~$X(t)\subset F(t,X(t))$ for all $t\in T;$\\[3pt] {\rm(iii)} $d_H(X_0,X(t_0))\le e\bigl(X_0,F(t_0,X(t_0))\bigr)$. \smallbreak In addition, if $X_0\subset F(t_0,X_0)$, then {\rm(iii)} can be replaced by $X(t_0)=X_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform excess-variation control plus a uniform contraction in the second variable yields a bounded-variation compact-valued solution of the functional inclusion with prescribed initial value.

there is a number $0\le\mu<1$ such that
there is a multifunction $K:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ such that
